text: Benito Mussolini, editor of the Italian Socialist Party’s newspaper Avanti!, breaks with the party by calling for Italy to enter the First World War, starts his own paper and is expelled. This turn from socialism to nationalism set him on the road to Fascism.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Benito Mussolini
World War I Document Archive (Brigham Young University Library), Benito Mussolini biography

method: Opened Britannica, Benito Mussolini; BYU WWI Document Archive biography of Mussolini
problem: Core facts supported, but calling the 1914 break ‘usually treated as the starting point of Fascism’ overstates it (Fascism is usually dated from the 1919 founding). Softened; added his new paper; added a second source.

text: Mussolini founds the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento (Italian Combat Leagues) in Milan with about a hundred followers, among them war veterans and former shock troops, Futurist artists and ex-socialists. The name comes from the fasces, the bundle of rods that stood for authority in ancient Rome, and gives the movement the word fascism.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, fasci di combattimento
AGI, Nicola Graziani, Cento anni fa nasceva il fascismo (23 March 2019)

method: Opened Britannica, fasci di combattimento (March 1919, Milan, name from Roman fasces); AGI, Nicola Graziani, 23 March 2019 (date, Piazza San Sepolcro, about 100 founders)
problem: ‘Mostly war veterans and nationalists’ is not supported: the founders were about a hundred arditi (ex-shock troops), Futurists and ex-socialists. Britannica gives only ‘March 1919’, so added AGI for the exact date.

method: Opened German History in Documents and Images, NSDAP Party Program (1920): Munich, 24 Feb 1920, DAP renamed NSDAP, Greater Germany, Versailles, German blood, nationalization of trusts

Opened Britannica, March on Rome: king refused to sign Facta’s state-of-siege decree, asked Mussolini to form a cabinet on 29 Oct. Britannica dates the march 28–30 Oct; 27–31 Oct (mobilization to Rome parade) is a common wider span and acceptable
Opened USHMM, Beer Hall Putsch: 8–9 Nov 1923, clash with police at Odeonsplatz, treason conviction, Landsberg, dictated Mein Kampf vol. 1
Opened Britannica, Matteotti Crisis: June 1924 murder by Fascist thugs after denouncing election violence; 3 Jan 1925 speech accepting responsibility; move to dictatorship
Opened USHMM, The Nazi Rise to Power: 20 May 1928, 2.6 percent

text: To crush resistance in Cyrenaica (eastern Libya), Italian forces deport 100,000–110,000 people, mostly women, children and the elderly, with their herds into desert concentration camps. Historian Ali Abdullatif Ahmida says about two-thirds of them died there; Italian historian Emilio Gentile counts about 50,000 deaths in the repression, and the exact toll is uncertain.

sources.cite: MERIP, Genocide, historical amnesia and Italian settler colonialism in Libya: an interview with Ali Abdullatif Ahmida (2022)
Wikipedia, Italian concentration camps in Libya (secondary)

method: Opened MERIP interview with Ahmida (100,000–110,000 deported with herds; two-thirds perished); Wikipedia, Italian concentration camps in Libya (1929–1934; mostly women, children, elderly; Gentile about 50,000)
problem: The ‘40,000 to 70,000’ range is unattributed and its low end was not found on any opened page (Wikipedia gives 50,000–70,000, unsourced). Replaced with named estimates. Wikipedia remains a secondary placeholder; Ahmida’s 2020 book is still the better replacement.

text: In the last German election with more than one party for 16 years, held amid arrests and intimidation after the Reichstag fire, the Nazis win almost 44 percent (43.9 in the official count). They reach a majority only together with their conservative nationalist partners.

sources.cite: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, The Nazi Rise to Power
Deutscher Bundestag, Kalenderblatt: Reichstagswahl 5 March 1933 (2023)
Deutsches Historisches Museum, LeMO: Reichstagswahl 1933

method: Opened USHMM, The Nazi Rise to Power (almost 44 percent); Bundestag Kalenderblatt 2023 (43.9 percent; last vote with more than one party competing for 16 years; NSDAP depended on the DNVP); DHM LeMO (terror, KPD driven underground; majority only with the Kampffront Schwarz-Weiß-Rot)
problem: ‘Last multi-party election before the war’ is wrong in framing: it was the last multi-party national election in Germany for 16 years (until 1949), not just before the war. ‘Coalition passes 50 percent’ kept in substance as ‘majority only with partners’ (the exact combined share was not on an opened page). Added sources.

text: The Reichstag passes the Enabling Act, letting the government make laws without parliament. It wins the two-thirds majority it needs after all 81 Communist deputies and 26 Social Democrats are kept from their seats and SA and SS men fill the hall; only the Social Democrats vote against.
method: Opened USHMM, The Enabling Act: 23 March 1933; 81 Communists and 26 of 120 Social Democrats kept from their seats; SA and SS in the chamber; only SPD voted no
problem: ‘The rules were manipulated’ is not on the cited page, and ‘passes only because’ is a stronger causal claim than the source makes. Rewritten to the facts USHMM gives.

text: The Nuremberg Laws strip German Jews of citizenship rights and ban marriage and sexual relations between Jews and other Germans. Nazi rules defined a Jew by ancestry, for example having three or more grandparents born into the Jewish community, whatever the person’s own faith.
method: Opened USHMM, Nuremberg Laws: 15 Sept 1935; Reich Citizenship Law; marriage and sex ban; Jews defined by ancestry (three or more grandparents born into the Jewish religious community), not by their own faith
problem: ‘Defining Jews by their grandparents’ religion’ is a loose shorthand: the laws defined Jews by supposed race and ancestry, using the grandparents’ membership of the Jewish community, regardless of the person’s own religion.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Italo-Ethiopian War
Rainer Baudendistel, Force versus law: the ICRC and chemical warfare in the Italo-Ethiopian war, 1935–1936, International Review of the Red Cross (1998)
Lina Grip and John Hart, The use of chemical weapons in the 1935–36 Italo-Ethiopian War, SIPRI (2009)

method: Opened Britannica, Italo-Ethiopian War (3 Oct 1935; Addis Ababa 5 May 1936; sanctions ineffective); IRRC, Baudendistel 1998 (mustard gas bombs); SIPRI, Grip and Hart 2009 (air bombs then aerial spray tanks; both states parties to the 1925 Geneva Protocol)
problem: Source addition only: neither cited page says the gas was sprayed from aircraft or that Italy was bound by the 1925 Protocol; SIPRI does.

text: A secret Japanese army unit in Manchuria carries out lethal human experiments from 1933; officially set up in 1936 and later known as Unit 731, it also developed biological weapons. Specialists widely accept that about 3,000 prisoners were killed at its Pingfang base near Harbin.
method: Opened Tsuneishi Keiichi, Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus (2005): experiments from autumn 1933 at Beiyinhe; officially set up 1936 as the Epidemic Prevention and Water Supply Department; Pingfan completed autumn 1939; about 3,000 killed there, ‘widely accepted among specialists’
problem: ‘Known from 1936 as Unit 731’ is inaccurate: in 1936 it was officially set up under another name (Epidemic Prevention and Water Supply Department); the Unit 731 designation came later.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Spain: The Civil War
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Spanish Civil War (summary)

method: Opened Britannica, Spain: The Civil War (rising began in Morocco 17 July 1936 and spread to the mainland; Franco led the Army of Africa; German, Italian and Soviet aid); Britannica summary (Popular Front government; foreign aid)
problem: Source addition only: the summary page gives no July date; the full Britannica Spain history section does.

text: After a grenade attack on Viceroy Rodolfo Graziani, Italian forces and Fascist militia kill residents across Addis Ababa for three days. Estimates of the dead range from about 3,000 (historians Angelo Del Boca and Anthony Mockler) to about 19,000 (Ian Campbell, 2017) and 30,000 (Ethiopian sources).
method: Opened History Today review by R. J. B. Bosworth (19–21 Feb 1937; Campbell about 19,000); Wikipedia, Yekatit 12 (Del Boca and Mockler about 3,000; Campbell about 19,200; Ethiopian sources 30,000)
problem: Anthony Mockler is a British writer, not an Italian historian; only Angelo Del Boca is Italian.

text: Aircraft of the German Condor Legion, joined by Italian planes, bomb the Basque town of Guernica (Gernika), killing many civilians. The toll is disputed: the Basque government recorded 1,654 deaths in 1937 and historian Xabier Irujo argues for 2,000 or more, while Spanish air force general Jesús Salas put it at about 120 and many accounts give 120 to 300.

sources.cite: Xabier Irujo, The nature and rationale of the Gernika bombing, The Volunteer (ALBA), 2013
Euskal Kazeta, Bombing of Guernica: the number of dead revised (interview with Xabier Irujo, 2024)
European Network Remembrance and Solidarity, Bombing of Guernica

method: Opened ALBA Volunteer, Xabier Irujo 2013 (Condor Legion with Italian planes; Basque government 1,654; Jesús Salas about 120; many accounts 120–250); Euskal Kazeta 2024 interview with Irujo (at least 2,000; common range 100–300); ENRS page (hundreds killed, no figures)
problem: ‘Killing hundreds’ conflicts with the low estimates the record itself quotes, and the estimates are not attributed. Named who made each figure.

text: After capturing Nanjing on 13 December 1937, Japanese troops kill surrendered soldiers and civilians on a mass scale, with widespread rape, looting and arson. Estimates of the dead depend on the area, period and victims counted: China’s government gives 300,000 or more, the postwar Tokyo tribunal more than 100,000 (in its verdict on General Matsui), and Japanese historians from about 40,000 (Hata Ikuhiko) to 160,000–170,000 (Kasahara Tokushi).
method: Opened Britannica, Nanjing Massacre (13 Dec 1937 capture; surrendered soldiers and civilians killed; tens of thousands of rapes; looting and arson; most estimates 100,000 to over 300,000); Wikipedia, Death toll of the Nanjing Massacre (estimates by who and on what scope)
problem: Standards require naming who made each estimate; the record gives an unattributed range and omits serious lower scholarly estimates (for example Hata Ikuhiko about 40,000).

Opened USHMM timeline, Munich Agreement: 29–30 Sept 1938; Germany, Italy, Britain, France; Czechoslovakia not a party

text: Madrid falls on 28 March 1939 and Franco declares the war over on 1 April; Britannica puts the war’s dead at about 500,000. Estimates of killings by Nationalists and the Franco regime during and after the war range from about 80,000 by 1943 (a conservative figure cited by Britannica) to about 150,000 (Paul Preston), against about 50,000 killings in the Republican zone.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Spanish Civil War (summary)
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Spain: The Civil War
Maclean’s, review of Paul Preston, The Spanish Holocaust

method: Opened Britannica summary (Madrid fell 28 March 1939; about 500,000 died); Britannica, Spain: The Civil War (conservative estimates about 80,000 Nationalist political killings to 1943; terror continued after the war); Maclean’s review of Preston (about 50,000 Republican-zone victims; Nationalist killings probably three times as many)
problem: The 130,000–150,000 range is unattributed and omits the lower conservative estimate (about 80,000) that Britannica cites. Named the estimators. The 1 April declaration is standard but was not on an opened page.

text: Romania’s Iron Guard rises against its partner in government, General Ion Antonescu. Antonescu crushes the revolt with German army support, and during the three days of violence Guardists murder 127 Jews in Bucharest, according to Yad Vashem.

sources.cite: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Romania
Yad Vashem, This Month in Holocaust History: January 1941

method: Opened USHMM, Romania (21 Jan 1941, three days, Antonescu won with German army support, ‘dozens’ murdered at the Bucharest slaughterhouse); Yad Vashem, This Month in Holocaust History, January 1941 (127 Jews murdered in the three-day riots)
problem: ‘Dozens of Jews’ understates the pogrom: USHMM’s ‘dozens’ refers only to the slaughterhouse killings; Yad Vashem gives 127 Jews murdered in all.
